title: Teacher notes: Mawhiba Grade 9, Unit 3 Linear functions and relations, Activity 2 Paired variables (Tasks 1 and 2), one session of about 40 minutes. Crews of four form before the session (Grapher, Algebraist, Checker, Reporter; roles rotate each task; stuck ladder: re-read, ask your crew, ask another crew, then the teacher). Advanced performance characteristics to develop: tolerate ambiguity and work with inexact relationships; show insight into the nature of different types of linear relationships in mathematics and science. Reminder: scatter graphs from Activity 1 plot paired observations that may show a relationship; open by asking why it is useful to present data this way (visualise relationships, spot outliers, line of best fit gives an estimate, predictions can be tested, informs further hypotheses). All data on the slides are model values.
journey: Teacher notes: four stations, 40 minutes (Match it 8, Read it 14, Judge it 8, Apply and present 10). Each station zooms in as students arrive; no ability labels, every crew starts at station 1. Pre-session home task covered independent and dependent variables and exact and inexact relationships, so spend no more than two minutes on definitions. Materials: the 3-page worksheet, a ruler, a sharp pencil, a spreadsheet or GeoGebra if allowed.
t1: Teacher notes: Task 1, minutes 1 to 8. Cut-up cards labelled Unit 3 Activity 2 Task 1 Variables (eighteen cards, nine pairs). Definitions: independent variables answer the question What do I change? Dependent variables answer What do I observe? Example if needed: in a lift the number of people is changed and the total weight is recorded. Let students work without interruption, then pairs join fours to compare and explain context and reasons. Possible pairings from the Guide: number of people in a lift and total weight of passengers; temperature and seedling growth; time in months and children's heights; mileage and petrol consumption; number of TVs and life span; time in hours and virus multiplication; time in years and radioactive decay; pressure and wind speed; amount of fertiliser applied to a crop whilst growing and the crop yield produced. There is more than one way of pairing the cards, so accept any pairing with a justified context. What if (gold strip): temperature could be paired with seedling growth or with wind speed in a weather context; time in hours could pair with virus multiplication or with seedling growth. Verbal misconceptions: the independent variable is the one that is easier to measure; the dependent variable always goes second in time; a pair must be a causal pair (number of TVs and life span are associated, not causal; a third variable such as wealth could sit behind both). Adaptive routing: if >30% of crews cannot start, give the lift example and re-ask the two questions; crews that finish early write for each pair which variable goes on the x-axis and why.
t2: Teacher notes: Task 2, minutes 9 to 14 (part 1 of 2). Show the three graphs and contexts, in pairs then fours, using the vocabulary: exact linear relationship, inexact linear relationship, experimental errors, limited assumptions, complex assumptions. Graph A (model values, adapted from the Guide's car-hire graph): hiring a car in Jeddah costs SAR 280 a day with the first 100 km included, then SAR 0.80 per extra km, so cost C = 0.8d + 280 for d km over 100. Every point lies exactly on the line: for example (10, 288) and (60, 328) give gradient (328 − 288) ÷ (60 − 10) = 0.8 and intercept 288 − 0.8 × 10 = 280. This is an EXACT linear relationship with few, simple assumptions (once the contract is agreed any difference should be marginal). Graph B: a spring stretched by added masses; ideal length 10 + 0.04 × mass, but the measured lengths differ by up to 0.4 cm: an INEXACT linear relationship caused by EXPERIMENTAL ERRORS (reading the ruler, parallax) and LIMITED assumptions (the spring is not stretched past its elastic limit). Graph C: dates harvested per palm against fertiliser; the harvest rises, levels off and falls, so there is a weak, curved or inexact linear relationship with COMPLEX assumptions (soil, water, heat, pests, palm age all interact). Verbal misconceptions: exact means real data, inexact means the experiment was done badly; a high correlation means exact; a model with no complex assumptions must be simple physics. Adaptive routing: if >30% call graph B exact, ask whether any dot sits off the line; if >30% struggle with graph C, ask what else besides fertiliser changes the harvest.
t3: Teacher notes: Task 2, minutes 15 to 22 (part 2 of 2). Graph B data (mass in g, length in cm): (50, 12.2), (100, 13.8), (150, 16.3), (200, 17.7), (250, 20.4), (300, 21.9), (350, 24.2), (400, 26.1), (450, 27.8), (500, 30.3). A line of best fit is y = 0.04x + 10 (gradient 0.04 cm per gram, so every extra 100 g stretches the spring by 4 cm; intercept 10 cm is the natural length with no mass). The largest gap between a dot and the line is 0.4 cm, so the relationship is strong but INEXACT. What if (gold strip): 5 kg is 5000 g, and the line predicts 10 + 0.04 × 5000 = 210 cm, which is impossible for a real spring because it would pass its elastic limit and stay stretched; the line is only trusted inside the range of the readings (50 g to 500 g). Done when: the crew can name the relationship (inexact linear), give a reason (dots scatter about the line, experimental errors), and interpret the gradient and intercept in context. Verbal misconceptions: reading the intercept as the length after 50 g; swapping the axes (length is the dependent variable because it is what we observe); believing the line is wrong because dots are off it. Adaptive routing: if >30% cannot interpret the gradient, ask 'how much longer does the spring get for 100 g?'; crews that finish early compare the three graphs by listing the assumptions behind each.
claims: Teacher notes: judge the claims, minutes 23 to 30. Claim A: FALSE. Graph B has dots off the line but a strong linear pattern; inexact linear relationships are very common and useful, and the model need not touch every dot. Claim B: FALSE as written, or SOMETIMES. Several pairings can be justified (temperature could be paired with seedling growth or with wind speed in a weather context), so the answer depends on the context chosen; require crews to state their context. Claim C: FALSE. The line gives 10 + 0.04 × 5000 = 210 cm at 5000 g, beyond the readings (50 g to 500 g) and past the elastic limit of any real spring. Assumption checks: does a model need to touch every dot; which context did I choose; does the spring still behave the same far beyond the readings. Plenary: which graph gave the strongest evidence (the exact car-hire graph) and how an inexact graph can still support a useful prediction inside its range. Verbal misconceptions: 'one counter-example is not enough'; 'exact and strong are the same'. Adaptive routing: if >30% mark Claim C true, ask them to compute the length at 5000 g and imagine the spring.
apply: Teacher notes: apply and present, minutes 31 to 40. Model values, not real charger data. Charge (%) against time (min): (0, 8), (10, 23), (20, 38), (30, 52), (40, 66), (50, 78), (60, 87). 1) Independent: charging time (what I change); dependent: battery charge (what I observe). 2) Using the first five readings, the points (10, 23) and (30, 52) give gradient (52 − 23) ÷ (30 − 10) = 1.45 and intercept 23 − 1.45 × 10 = 8.5, so y = 1.45x + 8.5; the other early readings are within 1 percentage point of this line. 3) At 25 minutes: 1.45 × 25 + 8.5 = 44.75, about 45%. 4) What if 90 minutes: the line gives 1.45 × 90 + 8.5 = 139%, which is impossible (a battery cannot exceed 100%); the later readings already fall below the line (at 60 minutes the line says 95.5% but the reading is 87%), because the charger slows down as the battery fills. So the relationship is inexact and linear only for the first 40 minutes or so; the assumptions are complex (battery management, temperature, charger power). Presentation: two reporters, one minute each. Mawhiba record: tick a value shown today and add evidence to the cumulative record. Verbal misconceptions: using all seven dots for one line; reading 139% as a valid answer; calling it exact because the first dots are close. Adaptive routing: if >30% mix up the variables, return to the two questions on slide 3.
